verdicts.trueWording: no one is worse at recognizing kin than our torturer hero
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211207124453id_ of 003055.html (live host timed out). Rex Lycanthrosaurus, Sat Oct 7 2006, thread '(urth) Thecla's genealogy folio'. Quote exact, in the long body paragraph beginning 'Well, I'd be lying'. The preceding sentence says Severian may be misinterpreting Thecla's stirring, so kin-recognition is named as the first-person narrator's specific blind spot. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: This shared facial characteristic may be Wolfe's way
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211205043249id_ of 003057.html. Roy C. Lackey, Thu Oct 12 2006. Quote exact; the sentence continues to name a genetic link. Body paragraph 3 as claimed. The two characters are Thea (often-mentioned heart-shaped face, hence a sharp chin) and Severian (sharp chin confirmed to Cyriaca); Lackey offers the blood relation as inference, not as something the books state — 'If this is correct, it also avoids the incest issue.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Nothing at all was mentioned about Catherine's height
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211207113027id_ of 058679.html. Roy C. Lackey, Fri Oct 13 2006. Quote exact; the same sentence adds that this is unusual for Severian to omit, which supports the 'detail the narrator habitually supplies' limb. The omission is raised inside the argument for Catherine's exultant status (the sentence immediately following turns on her class explaining Severian's height), so the absence functions as evidence about her. Located in the fifth body paragraph, as claimed.

verdicts.trueWording: Can you hear the difference in spelling between the spoken
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211207113027id_ of 058679.html, same message, body paragraph 3 as claimed. Quote exact; the sentence names the two spellings and the next sentence says Lackey cannot hear it and doubts Severian could. The page names Severian as the character who cannot hear the distinction (Ouen speaks the name); the claim's plural 'characters' generalises that, and the substance — a spelling distinction inaudible inside the spoken scene — is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: I don't see any indication in the text prior to this scene
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211207113027id_ of 058679.html, body paragraph 2 as claimed. Quote exact; the sentence continues that nothing shows Severian thought the maid might be his mother. Paragraph 1 establishes that Severian questions Ouen about a 'dark woman', and this paragraph concludes he must have arrived with a prior notion the text never records — Lackey himself supplying the missing premise. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Exultants weren't usually buried in the necropolis at all.
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211205044657id_ of 003166.html. Roy C. Lackey, Fri Oct 20 2006. Quote exact, in the reply block answering bsharp's burial argument, as the claim's locator says. The two following sentences (private estates, so no family plot on the hill) make burial custom by class the evidence against the woman in the coffin — the body Vodalus takes — being a missing exultant. Supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Severian's manuscript was not a daily journal or diary.
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211205044657id_ of 003166.html, final body paragraph as claimed. Quote exact; the next sentence states he wrote it all ten years after the events, and the paragraph closes by noting he had already had both later memories ten years before writing the 'piling pebbles' sentence — the retrospective-composition limb and the after-acquired-knowledge limb both supported.

verdicts.trueWording: ten times in about three pages
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211205050550id_ of 003175.html. Roy C. Lackey, Sat Oct 21 2006, body paragraph 3 as claimed. Quote exact; the count is of Severian's persistence in calling the woman a 'maid' across his elevation feast. Lackey then gives Webster's 'girl or young unmarried woman / virgin' and says that many references are hard to dismiss and suggest she cannot be the pregnant Catherine — the count read as a planted signal. Supported.

verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211207122316id_ of 003066.html. 'b sharp', Sun Oct 15 2006, body paragraph 5 as claimed. Quote exact (misspelling 'cooly' is the source's); the sentence completes 'as though she was very familiar with the ritual', and the paragraph concludes she is the real Catherine. verdicts.trueWording: I just can't ignore the circular connection between four characters
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211207120650id_ of 003094.html. 'b sharp', Tue Oct 17 2006. Quote exact. The list that follows supplies every named category — dark hair and pale gown (woman in the coffin), hair, gown, olive complexion and oval face (woman on the Path of Air), dark complexion and still-water face (the Katharine maid), hair and face (Valeria) — and the next paragraph builds a full covert life story from them. All limbs supported.

The stretch of institutional history is specified by the preceding run of questions — when she began the role, whether it was the same maid in Gurloes's boyhood, whether it ended when Severian left, whether she was there for Eata's two feasts. verdicts.trueWording: The guild masters knew damn well who the maid was
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture 20211207120326id_ of 058830.html. Quote exact; the sentence continues 'and where she came from; the ritual could not take place without their cooperation', and the next sentence says they knew who Severian's mother was — both limbs supported. Locator correction: this is the seventh of nine body paragraphs, not the penultimate one (two eidolon paragraphs follow).

Raw Wayback capture 20211207111751id_ of 003230.html. Roy C. Lackey, Thu Oct 26 2006, final body paragraph as claimed. Quote exact; the sentence glosses bear as 'to carry; transport' and the next says that followed by 'by' it does not mean having given birth. The quoted Wolfe sentence at the head of the message ('borne by Catherine in a cell of the oubliette') is the disputed one, and Lackey's whole point is that the maternity reading turns on that single word. Supported.
